3 Forces and energy

3.1 Forces and motion

Key words: balanced · change direction · direction · force · opposite · slow down · speed up · unbalanced

Balanced or unbalanced?

Look at any object that is not moving. You may think that if an object is not moving, no forces are acting on it. This is not true.

The force of gravity pulls the rock towards the centre of the Earth. This force is called its weight. The rock does not move downwards because the ground pushes up on the rock. This upward push is the contact force.

These two forces are balanced. Balanced means the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.

There can be more than two forces acting on the rock. Imagine the wind is blowing. The wind pushes the rock from one side, but the rock does not move sideways because the push from the wind is balanced by friction between the rock and the ground.

Forces are shown on a force diagram. In a force diagram, the arrows show the size and direction of each force. The longer the arrow, the bigger the force. So when you draw balanced forces, make the arrows the same length and point them in opposite directions.

Starting to move

Now imagine the rock is pushed with a much larger force than the wind, such as a push from a large vehicle.

The pushing force is now larger than friction. The sideways forces are unbalanced, so the rock starts to move in the direction of the larger sideways force.

The rock still does not move up or down, because the up and down forces are still balanced.

Slowing down

Unbalanced forces can also make a moving object slow down. A parachute makes a falling object slow down.

When the object is falling quickly, the parachute causes a force of air resistance that is larger than the weight of the object. The forces are unbalanced, so the object slows down.

As the object slows, the air resistance decreases. Eventually air resistance equals weight, the forces are balanced again, and the object falls at a constant speed.

Changing direction

Unbalanced forces can also make an object change direction.

When the ball hits the racket, the ball pushes on the racket and the racket pushes on the ball. To send the ball back in the opposite direction, the hitting force on the ball must be larger than the force from the ball on the racket.

Planets orbit the Sun because of the force of gravity. The force of gravity on a planet is a constant, unbalanced force.

When an object moves in a circle, its direction is always changing. A constant unbalanced force is needed to keep an object moving in a circle.

An aeroplane flying at a constant speed in a straight line has four forces acting on it: lift and weight are balanced, and thrust and drag are balanced.

Summary

  • When forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, the forces are balanced.
  • Balanced forces cause no change in movement.
  • When forces are not equal in size, and/or act in directions that are not opposite, the forces are unbalanced.
  • Unbalanced forces cause a change in movement: speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.
Size of forcesDirection of forcesBalanced or unbalancedChange in movement
EqualOppositeBalancedNone
EqualNot oppositeUnbalancedChange of direction
Not equalOppositeUnbalancedIncrease or decrease speed
Not equalNot oppositeUnbalancedChange of speed and of direction
Remember: an object that is not moving still has forces acting on it. They are simply balanced.

3.2 Speed

Key words: average speed · calculate · constant · m/s · metres per second · speed

Units of speed

There are many different units of speed. The speed of ships is often measured in knots, and aeroplanes often use Mach. Some countries set road speed limits in kilometres per hour, others in miles per hour.

To avoid confusion, scientists use standard units in all countries. The standard unit of speed is the metre per second, written m/s.

The word per means 'in each'. So metres per second means the number of metres travelled in each second. A horse running at a speed of 15 m/s travels 15 metres in each second.

Calculating speed

Think of a bus that travels 100 m in 20 s. How many metres does it travel in each 1 second?

number of metres travelled in each second = total distance travelled ÷ total time

The number of metres travelled in each second is the speed, so:

speed = distance ÷ time

For the bus: speed = 100 m ÷ 20 s = 5 m/s

The speed of an object during a journey is not always constant. Constant means not changing. When the speed changes, we use the term average speed. Average speed is calculated in exactly the same way.

Using the formula triangle

The same equation can be rearranged to find distance or time:

  • distance = speed × time
  • time = distance ÷ speed

Worked example 1. Marcus rides his bicycle at 4 m/s for 60 s. How far does he go?

distance = speed × time = 4 × 60 = 240 m

Worked example 2. Sofia is in a car travelling at 35 m/s. How long will the car take to travel 2100 m?

time = distance ÷ speed = 2100 ÷ 35 = 60 s

Worked example 3. An aeroplane travels 2500 km in 5 hours. What is its speed?

speed = distance ÷ time = 2500 ÷ 5 = 500 km/h

The units you put in decide the units you get out. If the distance is in km and the time is in hours, the speed comes out in km/h. Unless you are told otherwise, always work in metres, seconds and metres per second.

Remember: in every calculation, show the steps of your working and include the correct unit with your answer.

3.3 Describing movement

Key words: at rest · distance–time graph · sketch · stationary

Distance–time graphs

Scientists use graphs to describe how two variables are related. To describe the movement of an object, plot the distance travelled on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. A graph like this is called a distance–time graph.

Graphs are more useful than words for describing movement because:

  • it is easier to see trends and patterns
  • you can read any value of distance or time during the journey
  • other values, such as speed, can be calculated from the graph
  • information about the whole journey can be seen at once.

This graph shows the journey of a car from a starting position A to a destination C, and then back to A. Look at each of the four sections in turn.

  1. A to B — constant speed away from the start. The car travels the same distance in each second, so the distance from the start increases steadily with time. The line is straight and sloping upwards.
  2. At B — stationary. The car stops. Stationary means not moving, with a speed of zero; you can also say the car is at rest. The distance from the start does not change, but time still passes. The line is straight and horizontal.
  3. B to C — faster constant speed. The car travels a greater distance in each second than it did between A and B, so the line is straight, sloping upwards and steeper.
  4. C back to A — returning. The distance from the start decreases with time. The line is straight and sloping downwards.

A sketch graph does not need numbers on its axes. It only has to show the correct shape.

Reading values from a graph

When a distance–time graph does have values on the axes, you can use it to calculate speed. Read the distance from the vertical axis and the time from the horizontal axis, then use speed = distance ÷ time.

A train travels from station P to station R, a distance of 2000 m, in 200 s. It waits at R for 140 s, then returns to P in 100 s.

  • Speed from P to R = 2000 ÷ 200 = 10 m/s
  • Speed from R back to P = 2000 ÷ 100 = 20 m/s

The return line is steeper because the train is travelling faster.

Remember: on a distance–time graph, a steeper line means a faster speed, and a horizontal line means the object is stationary.

3.4 Turning forces

Key words: lever · moment · newton metre · pivot · turn

Turning effects of forces

When you push down on a door handle, the handle turns. When you push down on a bicycle pedal, the pedal turns. When you pull a door, the door turns towards you. These are all forces that cause an object to turn.

The object that turns is called a lever. The point around which the lever turns is called the pivot.

When you bend your arm, the arm acts as a lever and your elbow is the pivot. The human body has many levers and pivots.

Calculating moments

The moment of a force describes the turning effect of that force. The moment depends on two things:

  • the size of the force — the bigger the force, the bigger the moment
  • the distance from the pivot to where the force acts — the greater the distance, the greater the moment.
moment = force × distance

Here, distance means the distance from the pivot to the position where the force acts.

The unit of force is the newton (N) and the unit of distance is the metre (m), so the unit of moment is the newton metre, written N m. Use an upper case N and a lower case m.

Worked example 1. A pulling force of 35 N is needed to open a door. The distance from the handle to the hinges (the pivot) is 0.8 m. What is the moment?

moment = force × distance = 35 × 0.8 = 28 N m

Worked example 2. A weight of 20 N is held 0.25 m from the pivot at the elbow. What moment does the weight cause?

moment = force × distance = 20 × 0.25 = 5 N m

Balancing

A seesaw is a type of lever. People sit on either side of the pivot and make the lever turn one way and then the other.

A seesaw is balanced when the moments on both sides of the pivot are equal and opposite.

Worked example 3. Marcus has a weight of 600 N and sits 2 m from the pivot. Arun has a weight of 800 N. Where should Arun sit so the seesaw balances?

Marcus's moment = 600 × 2 = 1200 N m

For balance, Arun's moment must also be 1200 N m.

distance = moment ÷ force = 1200 ÷ 800 = 1.5 m from the pivot

Remember: a force pushing or pulling straight towards the pivot has no turning effect. The force must act at a distance from the pivot to produce a moment.

3.5 Pressure between solids

Key words: newtons per square metre · point · pressure · sharp · surface area

The pushing effect of a force

A knife works because the force used to push down on the clay causes pressure on the clay. You can think of pressure as the pushing effect of a force.

Suppose the clay is difficult to cut. You could:

  • increase the force on the knife — as the force increases, the pressure increases
  • use a sharper knife — a sharp knife has less surface area in contact with the clay, and as the area decreases, the pressure increases.
pressure = force ÷ area

The unit of force is the newton and the unit of area is the metre squared, so the unit of pressure is newtons per metre squared, N/m².

Smaller areas are sometimes measured in cm² or mm². If the area is in cm², the pressure is in N/cm². If the area is in mm², the pressure is in N/mm².

Large areas and small areas

Some things have large areas to decrease pressure; others have small areas to increase pressure.

A camel has large feet, so the force from its weight acts over a large area. The pressure on the sand is decreased, so the camel does not sink.

On a bed of nails, the weight of the person acts on many hundreds of sharp points, so the pressure from each nail is very small.

The end of a pin has a sharp point with a very small area. The pressure is increased, so the pin goes easily into wood or card.

Scissors have sharp blades. The area along each cutting edge is small, which increases the pressure and makes things easier to cut.

Calculating pressure

Worked example 1. An elephant has a weight of 50 000 N. The total area of all four feet is 0.4 m². What pressure does it exert on the ground?

pressure = force ÷ area = 50 000 ÷ 0.4 = 125 000 N/m²

The unit is N/m² because the area was given in m².

Worked example 2. A bicycle and rider together weigh 1000 N, supported equally on two tyres. The area of each tyre in contact with the ground is 5 cm². What pressure does each tyre exert?

weight on each tyre = 1000 ÷ 2 = 500 N

pressure = force ÷ area = 500 ÷ 5 = 100 N/cm²

The unit is N/cm² because the area was given in cm².

Worked example 3. A nail has a point of area 1.5 mm². A pressure of 50 N/mm² is needed for the nail to go into wood. What force is needed from the hammer?

force = pressure × area = 50 × 1.5 = 75 N

Remember: the unit of pressure comes from the units you put in. Force in N with area in cm² gives pressure in N/cm².

3.6 Pressure in liquids and gases

Key words: altitude · atmospheric pressure · collide · container · depth · sea level

Pressure in liquids

Look at the dam. Water comes out from two levels. The water coming out near the top comes out with less force. The water coming out from further down comes out with more force. This is because pressure in a liquid increases with depth.

The wall of the dam is wider at the bottom to make it stronger where the pressure from the water is greatest.

Pressure and depth in liquids

Why does pressure increase with depth?

As you go deeper in a liquid, there is more liquid above your position. The weight of this liquid, caused by gravity, pushes on the particles of the liquid below it. When the particles of the liquid are pushed, they move with more force.

The particles in a liquid move randomly in all directions, so the pressure in a liquid is equal in all directions at a given depth.

Pressure in gases

Before you blow up a balloon there is only a small volume of air inside it. The balloon is open at one end, so the pressure inside is the same as the pressure outside. As you blow air in, you are adding more gas particles.

Particles in a gas move randomly and collide with the walls of the container. Every time a particle collides with the wall, it exerts a small force on the wall.

The more particles there are in the gas, the more collisions happen with the walls, and so the total force on the walls increases. That force acts on an area, so it causes pressure. The pressure inside the balloon gets bigger as you blow in more air, pushing the walls of the balloon outwards.

The air inside this tyre is at low pressure — not enough to support the weight of the vehicle. If more air is put inside, more collisions happen with the inside walls, the pressure increases, and the tyre is pushed outwards so that it supports the vehicle.

Pressure and depth in gases

As with liquids, the pressure in a gas increases with depth. Altitude is height above sea level. The Earth's atmosphere is made of gases, and sea level is where the atmosphere is at its deepest. So atmospheric pressure is highest at sea level.

As you go higher in the atmosphere, two things change:

  • the number of particles in each cubic metre of air decreases, so the concentration of gas particles decreases
  • the weight of air above your position decreases.

Both changes make atmospheric pressure smaller at high altitude.

Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 100 000 N/m². That is like the weight of two large elephants pushing on every square metre of surface. We are not aware of it because we live in the atmosphere all the time, and the pressure inside our bodies is the same.

Effects of atmospheric pressure

The effect of atmospheric pressure can be shown by pumping the air out of a metal container.

  • Before the air is pumped out, the pressure inside the container equals the pressure outside.
  • When the air is pumped out, the pressure inside becomes close to zero, but the pressure outside does not change.
  • The container is crushed by the pressure of the air outside.

Pressure and temperature in gases

As the temperature of a gas increases, the speed of the particles increases. Particles travelling faster exert more force in each collision, and collide more often. So increasing the temperature of a gas in a sealed container increases its pressure.

A pressure cooker uses this effect. Water and food are put inside and the lid is sealed. When the water boils the steam cannot escape, so the pressure of the gas inside increases and the food cooks faster. A weight on top controls the pressure, and valves let steam escape once the required pressure is reached.

Remember: pressure in a gas can be increased in three ways — add more particles, make the container smaller, or raise the temperature.

3.7 Particles on the move

Key words: concentration · diffusion

Mixing gases

The particles in a gas move randomly. Both the speed of the particles and the direction of the particles are random.

If two gases are mixed in one container, the particles of each gas move randomly, so each gas spreads out to fill the container. This movement of the particles of each gas is called diffusion.

Diffusion is the overall random movement of particles from an area where they are in higher concentration to an area where they are in lower concentration. Concentration is the number of particles in a particular volume.
  1. At the start, the tap is closed. One gas is at high concentration on the left and zero concentration on the right. The other gas is at high concentration on the right and zero concentration on the left.
  2. The tap is opened and the gases start to spread out. At random, some particles of each gas pass through the space where the tap opens. Each gas is now at quite high concentration on its own side and low concentration on the other side.
  3. After some time the gases have completely diffused. There is equal concentration of both gases on both sides.

Diffusion stops when the concentrations are equal. However, the movement of individual particles does not stop when diffusion stops. Particles still cross from side to side — but now equal numbers cross each way, so there is no overall change.

Smelling food

Diffusion explains how you can smell food cooking. When food is heated, some particles in the food change state and become a gas. These gas particles move randomly and so spread out through the air by diffusion.

The smell gets stronger as you move closer to the food, because the concentration of the particles is higher the closer you get to the source of the particles. Many animals use this change in the strength of a smell to find food.

Mixing liquids

Diffusion also happens in liquids, because particles in a liquid also move at random.

When blue ink is added to water, the ink moves from the area of high concentration to the areas of low concentration, until it is completely diffused throughout the water.

Speed of diffusion

The speed of diffusion depends on two things:

  • the difference in concentration of the particles — the bigger the difference in the concentrations, the faster the diffusion
  • temperature — the higher the temperature, the faster the diffusion. Higher temperature makes particles move faster, so the particles can spread out faster.

For example, when you make a cup of tea the tea diffuses through the water. It diffuses faster in hot water than in cold water.

Remember: diffusion needs nothing to push the particles along. The particles were already moving at random; there are simply more of them starting in the crowded region, so more of them move out than move in.

Summary checklist

  • I can describe what is meant by balanced forces in terms of size and direction.
  • I can understand that forces can be acting on an object that is not moving.
  • I can recognise when forces are unbalanced.
  • I can list some of the effects of unbalanced forces.
  • I know and can use the equation that links speed, distance and time.
  • I can use the equation to calculate speed, distance or time when I know the other two quantities.
  • I know that the standard units are metres, seconds and metres per second.
  • I can calculate speeds using different units.
  • I can sketch a distance–time graph for an object moving at a constant speed away from a starting position.
  • I can sketch a distance–time graph for a stationary object.
  • I can sketch a distance–time graph for an object moving back towards a starting position.
  • I can tell whether an object is moving quickly, slowly or is stationary from a distance–time graph.
  • I can read values from a distance–time graph and use them to calculate speed.
  • I can understand that forces can cause turning effects.
  • I can understand what is meant by the term moment.
  • I know and can use the equation that links moment, force and distance.
  • I know the unit of moment.
  • I can understand that pressure is the pushing effect of a force.
  • I know and can use the equation that links pressure, force and area.
  • I can work out the unit of pressure from the units of force and area.
  • I can understand what causes pressure in a liquid and how it changes with depth.
  • I can understand what causes pressure in a gas.
  • I can understand how altitude affects atmospheric pressure.
  • I can understand how the quantity of gas in a container affects the pressure.
  • I can understand how the temperature of a gas in a closed container affects the pressure.
  • I know how to describe diffusion.
  • I can understand how diffusion happens in gases.
  • I can understand how diffusion happens in liquids.
  • I can understand that the speed of diffusion is affected by the difference in concentration and by the temperature.
